title: Three Handshakes

post.author: u/gull_point_keeper
post.title: I kept the radio at a lighthouse for 31 years. In Thursday's storm, my daughter's voice told me it was safe to go out.

blocks.text: I was the radio keeper at Gull Point light for 31 years. The lamp runs itself now, but I still live in the keeper's house and I still keep a log. On the old radio every exchange began the same way. *Gull Point calling Harbor, over.* *Harbor here, I hear you, over.* *Gull Point hears you, go ahead.* Three calls before one word of news. And after every message you waited for *received*. No *received*, you said it again.

Last year my grandson Theo put in a satellite dish and taught me the new way. Everything you send is cut into small numbered pieces called packets. They go up to a satellite and down to the mainland, about a quarter of a second each way. Some things travel by TCP, he said, and that's my old radio: three calls to open a connection, which he calls the handshake, a *received*, an ACK, for every packet, and anything not confirmed is sent again, so the far end can put it all back in order. Video calls travel by UDP. No calls first, no *received*, nothing sent twice.

On Thursday a storm sat on us all night. Theo's screen said the link was losing about one packet in five. At 2:00 the weather station sent its hourly file to the harbor. On a calm night that takes two seconds.
At 2:13 my daughter Ada video-called from the mainland. Her face froze and jumped. Her voice came in pieces. I wrote down what I heard:

02:00:00  weather file to Harbor   120 packets
02:00:41  weather file arrived     complete, in order, 29 packets sent again
02:13:40  video call, Ada          "Dad, ... safe to go out tonight."

I had my coat on before I knew it. The lamp room is 112 steps of wet iron up, and the light hasn't needed me in years. Then Ada rang back on the old phone line, frightened. What she had said was *Dad, it's not safe to go out tonight.*
The storm only took two words. It took the right two.

The weather file crossed the same storm and arrived with nothing missing. So why does a file of numbers come through whole while my daughter's voice gets torn? And the harbor wants more from us this winter. What should travel which way?

diagram.aria: Ada's video call at 2:13 AM, packet by packet, from Ada's phone through the satellite link to Gull Point. Packet 1, Dad, arrives. Packet 2, it's, and packet 3, not, are lost at the satellite link. Packets 4 to 8, safe, to, go, out, tonight, arrive. Nobody asks for packets 2 and 3 again. The keeper hears: Dad, ... safe to go out tonight.

Heard: Dad, ... safe to go out tonight.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Your old radio procedure is closer to the truth than Theo's diagram. Count the calls before the weather station says its first number, and how long each call takes on your link. Then imagine what waiting for *received* after every word would do to a phone call.

replies.author: u/gull_point_keeper
replies.text: Two calls there and back before the station may start, so half a second gone before the first number even leaves. And if Ada's call waited for *received* after every word, she would still be talking.

comments.author: u/coastwise_kat
comments.text: Fisherman here. Our video calls from the boat do the same in rough weather: frozen face, missing words, then suddenly live again. It never falls behind. It just skips. Our chart downloads never skip anything. They just take forever.

comments.author: u/packet_ghost
comments.text: The storm took packets from both. Only one of them noticed.

reply.prompt: The harbor wants two new things from Gull Point: the live wind speed on their screen every second during storms, and the full storm log, every reading, for the insurance people each morning. How should each one travel? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Send the live wind readings over UDP, since a late reading is useless and the next one is a second away. Send the storm log over TCP, since every reading must arrive, in order, even if it takes longer.
options.part2: Theo set it up that way. In Friday's gale the harbor's wind screen skipped a reading now and then, but it never froze and never fell behind: when a gust hit Gull Point, the harbor saw it about a quarter of a second later. The morning log arrived whole, all 86,400 readings, in order. One thing Theo can't explain. Every night at 3:00, something on the mainland opens a connection to the lighthouse, makes all three calls of the handshake, says nothing, and hangs up. Nobody at the harbor admits to sending it.
options.senior: Choose TCP or UDP by what a late or missing piece costs. Live readings: a late one is worthless, so don't wait for it. Records: a missing one is a disaster, so wait as long as it takes.

options.text: Send both over TCP. It never loses anything, so the harbor always gets the full picture.
options.verdict: Reliable, but late when it matters
options.part2: Both went over TCP. The log was perfect. The wind screen was not. Whenever the storm took a packet, every reading behind it waited in line until the lost one was sent again. The harbor's screen froze for a second or more, then raced through old readings to catch up. On Friday it showed calm air at Gull Point while the gust that tore our weather vane off had already passed.
options.senior: TCP hands data over strictly in order, so one lost packet holds up everything behind it until its copy arrives. For live data that's the wrong promise: you'd rather skip a reading than see an old one late.

options.text: Send both over UDP, and send every packet three times so at least one copy gets through.
options.verdict: Trade-off: triple the traffic, still no promise
options.part2: Theo tried it. The wind screen was fine, if busy. The storm log mostly arrived. But the satellite company charges for everything we send, so the bill tripled, and in Friday's worst hour all three copies of some packets were lost. The insurance people found 212 readings missing and asked what the wind did at 2:47 AM. We don't know.
options.senior: Sending copies makes loss less likely, not impossible, and it triples the traffic in calm weather too. If every piece must arrive, use TCP, which notices exactly what's missing and asks for that again.

options.text: Wait for calm weather and send everything then. Storms are when the link is worst.
options.verdict: Misses the point of a storm
options.part2: The harbor got lovely data on calm days and nothing during storms, which is the only time they wanted it. On Friday the wind screen sat blank for nine hours. The log arrived on Saturday afternoon, complete, and no use to the boats that had already gone out.
options.senior: The data you need most is often the data that can't wait. Pick a way of sending that copes with a bad link instead of hoping for a good one.

sim.title: Send Ada's message through the storm
sim.lede: You're the satellite link on the night of the storm. Ada's message is cut into 8 packets, one word each, numbered 1 to 8. Pick TCP or UDP and how many packets the storm eats, then send. Everything runs 4 times slower than real life so you can watch each packet. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: send with UDP at 20% and read what the keeper hears. Reset, switch to TCP and send again: watch the handshake, the lost packets sent again, and words held back until the gap fills. Compare when the first word arrives. Then push the storm to 50%.

explain.oneLine: Nothing chose those words. The storm dropped about one packet in five from everything. The weather file used TCP, which noticed and sent its lost packets again. Ada's call used UDP, which never looks back.

steps.title: Everything travels in packets.
steps.text: Data on a network is cut into packets: small pieces, each carrying a slice of the data plus a label saying where it's going. A real call sends many packets every second, each a sliver of sound. Packets travel separately. They can be lost (a storm garbles them, a busy machine throws them away) or arrive in a different order than they left. The network itself promises nothing. Any promise comes from the protocol on top: TCP or UDP.

steps.title: TCP opens with three calls.
steps.text: Before any data, TCP opens a connection with the three-way handshake. SYN: *calling, I'll start counting at 100.* SYN-ACK: *I hear you, I'll start at 900.* ACK: *I hear you too.* Each side picks a starting sequence number so both can count what they send. The sender may start right behind its ACK, so the handshake costs one full round trip before the first byte moves: on Gull Point's satellite link, about half a second.

steps.title: Every byte is numbered and confirmed.
steps.text: TCP numbers every byte it sends, and the receiver answers with acknowledgements, ACKs: *I have everything up to here.* If no ACK comes back before a timer runs out, the sender sends that piece again. That's a retransmission. Before TCP has measured the link, the timer is one second, and each time it runs out it doubles, so a struggling link isn't flooded with copies.

steps.title: TCP hands data over in order, so it waits.
steps.text: Packets that arrive early are held in a buffer until the missing one turns up, then everything is handed to the program in order. That's why the weather file was perfect, and why it took 41 seconds instead of two: each lost packet held up the ones behind it until its copy arrived, 29 times over. Engineers call this head-of-line blocking.

steps.title: UDP just sends.
steps.text: UDP has no handshake, no ACKs, no retransmission and no reordering. Each packet goes once, and the program gets whatever arrives, in whatever order. For a video call that's right: a word that arrives two seconds late is worse than a gap, so the call app skips it and stays live. Ada's *it's* and *not* fell into the storm, and nothing ever asked for them again.

diagram.aria: The weather file over TCP. The weather station and the harbor open a connection with the three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. Packet 1 arrives. Packet 2 is lost at the satellite link. Packet 3 arrives and is held back, waiting for packet 2. The harbor's ACK says it has 1 and 3 and needs 2. The station's timer for packet 2 runs out, it sends packet 2 again, and the harbor hands packets 1, 2 and 3 over in order.

steps.label: SYN: calling Harbor, I start at 100
SYN-ACK: I hear you, I start at 900
ACK: I hear you too. Here comes #1

explain.caption: Read top to bottom. Three calls open the connection before any data moves. Packet #2 is lost, so the harbor holds #3 back and says what it still needs. When the station's timer for #2 runs out with no ACK, it sends #2 again, and the harbor hands all three over in order. On Thursday this happened 29 times, which is why the file took 41 seconds.

fix.title: The fix: pick the transport by what lateness costs
fix.text: Ask one question about each kind of data: is a late piece still useful? If every piece must arrive, in order (files, logs, payments, web pages), use TCP and accept that loss shows up as delay. If a late piece is worthless because a newer one is already on its way (live voice, video, game positions, a live wind gauge), use UDP and let the program cover the gaps: a call app smooths over a missing sliver of sound, a wind screen just shows the next reading. Don't send copies of everything to fake reliability, and don't run live data over TCP and hope the link stays clean.

limits: UDP doesn't make a bad link good. Programs that use it have to handle loss themselves, for example by smoothing small gaps or lowering picture quality when loss climbs. When loss gets very high, a call still breaks up.

TCP's promise has a cost. On a lossy link it gets slow, and if packets keep vanishing it eventually gives up and reports the connection broken. Reliable means *eventually, or an error*, not *on time*.

Handshakes add up. Every new TCP connection pays a round trip before any data moves, so programs that open many short connections over a slow link feel it. That's why apps and browsers keep connections open and reuse them.

head: Transport
Good
Bad
rows: Every byte arrives, in order, or you get an error. The program never has to think about loss.
A round trip of handshake before any data. One lost packet delays everything behind it.
No setup and no waiting. Each packet is handed over the moment it arrives.
Lost packets stay lost, and order isn't kept. The program has to cope with gaps itself.

explain.seniorTake: Every network loses packets. The protocol only decides who pays: TCP makes you wait, UDP makes you live with the gap. Ask what a late piece is worth before you pick.

realWorld.title: RFC 9293: what TCP promises
realWorld.text: TCP's current specification is RFC 9293, published in August 2022, replacing the original RFC 793. It says TCP provides a reliable, in-order, byte-stream service to applications. Every byte has a sequence number, and acknowledgements are cumulative: acknowledging X means everything before X has arrived. It calls the opening exchange the three-way handshake, and explains that it's needed because sequence numbers aren't tied to a global clock.

realWorld.title: RFC 768: what UDP doesn't promise
realWorld.text: UDP's specification, RFC 768, dates from August 1980 and is very short. It says that delivery and duplicate protection are not guaranteed, and that applications needing ordered, reliable delivery of a stream of data should use TCP.

realWorld.title: RFC 6298: how long TCP waits before resending
realWorld.text: RFC 6298 sets TCP's retransmission timer. Until the sender has measured a round trip, the timer should be 1 second. Each time it runs out, the sender doubles it, backing off instead of flooding a struggling link.

realWorld.title: Why live calls choose UDP
realWorld.text: In *High Performance Browser Networking*, Ilya Grigorik explains that every new TCP connection costs a full round trip before any application data, and that a lost packet holds every later packet in the receiver's buffer until it's retransmitted. In the book's WebRTC chapter, on live audio and video in the browser, he writes that the need for timeliness over reliability is the main reason UDP is preferred for real-time data: people barely notice a few dropped samples, but they do notice delay.

asked: What's the difference between TCP and UDP, and when would you use each?
Walk me through the TCP three-way handshake. What does it cost?
interview.answer: TCP gives a reliable, ordered byte stream: a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) to agree on starting sequence numbers, ACKs for data received, retransmission when a timer runs out, and in-order delivery with buffering. The costs are a round trip to set up each connection and head-of-line blocking when packets are lost. UDP sends independent packets with no setup, no ACKs, no retransmission and no ordering. Use TCP when every byte matters (files, web pages, databases) and UDP when lateness is worse than loss (voice, video, games, live readings), and say that a program on UDP has to handle loss itself. Mention reusing connections to avoid paying the handshake again and again.

terms.def: A small piece of data sent across a network on its own, with a label saying where it's going. Messages and files are cut into packets and put back together at the far end.
An agreed set of rules for how two programs talk, like the radio's calling, over and received.
Here, the protocol that carries data between two programs across the network. TCP and UDP are the two common ones.
Transmission Control Protocol: opens a connection with a handshake, numbers every byte, waits for ACKs, resends what's lost and hands data over in order. Reliable, but loss shows up as delay.
User Datagram Protocol: sends each packet once, with no handshake, no ACKs, no resending and no reordering. Fast and simple. What's lost stays lost.
The three messages that open a TCP connection: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. They let both sides agree on starting sequence numbers. It costs one round trip.
Short for the three-way handshake: TCP's three calls before any data.
Synchronize: the first handshake message. The caller says it wants a connection and gives its starting sequence number.
The second handshake message: the receiver confirms the SYN and gives its own starting sequence number.
Acknowledgement: a message saying what has been received so far. TCP's version of the radio's received.
A reply confirming that data arrived. In TCP, acknowledging X means everything before X has arrived.
An ACK that also lists pieces that arrived out of order, so the sender resends only what's missing. TCP can use it when both sides agree.
The number TCP gives each byte it sends, so the receiver can spot gaps and put data back in order. Each side picks where its count starts.
The basic unit of computer data, enough to store one letter of plain text. TCP counts what it sends in bytes.
Data treated as one long, unbroken run of bytes. TCP delivers a byte stream: the program never sees the packets, just the bytes, in order.
Sending a packet again because no ACK came back in time. TCP does it. UDP never does.
How long TCP waits for an ACK before sending a packet again. It starts at 1 second before the link is measured and doubles each time it runs out.
The time for a message to go to the far end and for the answer to come back. About half a second on Gull Point's satellite link.
Delay: how long data takes to get from one place to another. A handshake adds a round trip of latency before any data.
Packets that never arrive, because a storm, a bad cable or a busy machine destroyed or dropped them. Usually given as a share, like one in five.
Handed to the program in the same order it was sent. TCP guarantees it. UDP doesn't.
Arriving in a different order than sent, for example packet 5 before packet 4, because packets can take slightly different times.
A waiting area in memory. TCP's receiver holds early packets in a buffer until the gap in front of them is filled.
When one lost packet holds up everything behind it, like a stalled car at a single-lane bridge. TCP's in-order promise causes it.
A second copy of the same packet arriving. UDP doesn't detect duplicates for you.
A network connection that bounces off a satellite far above the Earth. The long trip makes every round trip slow.
Data that is only useful right now, like a live call or the current wind speed. A late copy is worth little.
The browser feature for live audio and video calls between people, built for real-time data.
Request for Comments: the numbered documents that define internet standards, like RFC 9293 for TCP.
Numbers a system reports about itself over time, like requests per second or memory used.

atWork: Find one thing at work that sends live data (metrics, a voice or video feature, a game, live locations) and one that moves records (file uploads, a web page, a database). For each, find out whether it travels over TCP or UDP. On AWS, every security group rule names its protocol, TCP or UDP, next to the port, so an instance's inbound rules are a quick place to look. Then ask the case's question: if a packet is lost, is this data better late or missing? Note any place where the answer and the transport disagree.

recall.prompt: You're building a live map of delivery trucks that updates each truck's position every second. A teammate wants TCP so nothing is ever lost. What do you say?

keyIdeas.idea: A late position is useless: a newer one is a second away
TCP would hold everything up waiting for a lost packet
Use UDP and skip lost updates

recall.model: A position is only useful while it's fresh, and the next one is a second away. Over TCP, one lost packet would hold every later position in the buffer until it was resent, so the map would freeze and then jump through old positions. Use UDP and let the map skip a lost update and draw the next one. Keep TCP for the things that must all arrive, like the day's delivery records.

recall.prompt: What are the three messages of TCP's handshake, in order?
recall.why: The caller sends SYN with its starting number, the receiver answers SYN-ACK with its own, and the caller confirms with ACK. Only then can data flow, which is why it costs one round trip.

recall.prompt: In a storm, a file sent over TCP and a video call over UDP both lose 1 packet in 5. What happens?
options: The file arrives complete but slower. The call skips the lost pieces and stays live.
The call arrives complete. The file has gaps.
recall.why: TCP notices each lost packet and resends it, so the file is complete but delayed. UDP never resends, so the call loses those pieces and plays on.

recall.prompt: An app on a satellite link (about half a second for a round trip) opens 6 new TCP connections, one after another, each to fetch one small file. It feels slow even though the files are tiny. Why, and what would help?

keyIdeas.idea: Each new connection costs a handshake round trip before any data
Six handshakes add up to about 3 seconds of waiting
Reuse one connection, or open them at the same time

recall.model: Every new TCP connection pays a handshake, one round trip, before a single byte of the file can move. At half a second a round trip, six connections one after another spend about 3 seconds just shaking hands. Reuse one open connection for all six files, or at least open them at the same time, so the handshake is paid once instead of six times.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. Theo moved the harbor's wind screen to UDP and it's been perfect. Now the harbor wants the daily storm log, every reading for the insurance people, sent over the same UDP link, "since it works so well." Theo tested it on a calm night and all 86,400 readings arrived.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Should Theo do it? What happens on the next stormy night, and what should he use?

keyIdeas.idea: A calm night proves nothing: storms lose packets
UDP never resends or reorders, so the log will have holes

coldCase.model: Don't. The calm-night test only shows that nothing was lost when nothing was being lost. In a storm the link drops about one packet in five, and UDP never notices, never resends and never puts things back in order, so the insurance log would arrive with holes and nobody would know which readings were missing. Keep the live wind screen on UDP, where skipping is fine, and send the log over TCP, where every reading arrives in order, even if the storm makes it slow.
